FFS AMD

Construction cores, like Bulldozer, Piledriver, etc had the aim of giving users more multi-threaded performance at a low price at the expense of single threaded performance. The software took way too long to catch up with the hardware, and AMD really made a poor choice. Zen's approach is to offer similar single thread performance to Intel, but more multi-thread performance.

Construction cores did it via some weird core sharing, where each core shares parts of another core. In theory it makes a lot of sense, when your CPU is working, it's not using all of the CPU core. There's usually dormant parts that sit idle. Hyperthreading is the idea that you cram more stuff into each core to use the parts that aren't working. Obviously this doesn't do much if you have two threads that want to use the same part of a core. Construction core's idea was to split the cores, so that you have extra hardware and you hope that threads don't want to use the same part of the core. Construction core idea was basically to add another unit to each core, then marketing decided it should be an 8 core. Like I said, in theory, it sounds better than Hyperthreading since you're solving the problem with adding more CPU as opposed to cramming more stuff into an existing core. Sadly it didn't work out that way. Not to mention AMD targeted a low IPC, high clock speed design, which always ends in failure if the process you use to make your chip doesn't clock well enough. And original Bulldozer didn't clock well at all.

Zen is more of a high IPC, lower frequency design. I highly doubt we'll see 5ghz+ Zens when we do see 5ghz+ with Piledriver. But AMD won't have to depend on the process to have high clocks for performance. And they didn't sacrifice single threaded performance for multi-threaded performance.

But, the neat thing AMD is doing is that they made the cores a bit smaller than normal while still supposedly running well. But, when AMD competes in mid-range (like 6700k), AMD has a huge advantage. Most of 6700k (and similar) CPUs is GPU, display logic, etc. Zen won't have that as it's a pure CPU. So, you end up with a Zen 8 core CPU that's around the same size as an Intel 4 core with a GPU. Which means there's a very good chance that AMD can deliver an 8 core CPU that's around Intel in single thread, but it would be cost competitive with Intel quad core CPUs.

I have a lot of faith in AMD's strategy. Construction cores are way behind Intel in performance per clock. But if AMD fixes that while still offering a lot more cores for around the same price, it's going to be a really big win for them.
